title: Angles, Triangles and Scale
bigQuestion: How can a few facts about angles and lengths let us know things we cannot measure directly?

story.title: The Surveyor Who Measured the Earth with Shadows
story.kicker: More than two thousand years ago, a librarian used a well, a stick and a little geometry to measure the whole planet.
paragraphs: Eratosthenes ran the great library in Alexandria, Egypt, in the third century BCE. He read a report about a town far to the south called Syene, near where Aswan is today. On the longest day of the year, at noon, the sun there shone straight down a deep well and lit the water at the bottom. A vertical stick cast no shadow at all. The sun was directly overhead.

Eratosthenes knew that in Alexandria on that same day, a vertical stick did cast a shadow. He measured the angle between the stick and the edge of its shadow. It came to about 7 degrees, roughly one fiftieth of a full circle of 360 degrees. Why would the sun be straight overhead in one town and tilted in another on the same day at the same hour? Only because the ground itself curves. The Earth is round.

Then came the geometry. The sun is so far away that its rays reach both towns as parallel lines. A vertical stick points at the center of the Earth. So the angle between the stick and the sun's rays in Alexandria is the same as the angle at the Earth's center between the two towns. That is a fact about parallel lines cut by a crossing line, and you will prove it in this chapter. If the two towns are one fiftieth of a circle apart, then the distance between them is one fiftieth of the distance around the whole Earth.

He knew that distance. Travelers and royal surveyors had paced the road from Alexandria to Syene many times. Multiply it by 50 and you have the circumference of the Earth. His answer, in the units of his day, was remarkably close to the modern figure of about 40,000 kilometers. He never left Egypt. He never saw the Earth from above. He measured it with an angle, a distance and the idea that lines that are parallel make equal angles wherever you cross them.

That is the power of this chapter. Angles that sit next to each other, angles made by crossing lines, the three angles inside every triangle and the rule that lets a drawing stand in for a building: each is a small fact, and each lets you find something you could never reach with a ruler.
story.think: Eratosthenes needed two measurements: an angle and a distance. Which one do you think was harder to get right in his time, and why?

lessons.title: Adding to 90 or 180
lessons.mainIdea: Two angles are complementary if they add to 90 degrees and supplementary if they add to 180, and each fact lets you find a missing angle by subtracting.
reading: An *angle* measures how far one line turns from another, in degrees. A square corner is 90 degrees. A straight line is 180 degrees, because it is two square corners side by side. Those two numbers give us two important kinds of angle pairs.

Two angles whose measures add to 90 degrees are *complementary*. If a corner of a square is split by a diagonal line into a 35-degree angle and a second angle, the second one must be 90 − 35 = 55 degrees. Check: 35 + 55 = 90. The two angles do not have to touch. A 30-degree angle on one page and a 60-degree angle on another page are still complementary.

Two angles whose measures add to 180 degrees are *supplementary*. Picture a straight road with a side street branching off. The two angles the side street makes with the road add to 180. If one is 112 degrees, the other is 180 − 112 = 68 degrees. Check by adding: 112 + 68 = 180.

Students mix up the two words. One memory trick: C comes before S in the alphabet, and 90 comes before 180. Another common slip is subtracting from the wrong number, such as finding 90 − 112 and getting a negative angle. If your answer is negative or bigger than the total, you used the wrong pair.

words.d: the amount of turn between two lines that meet at a point, measured in degrees
two angles whose measures add to 90 degrees
two angles whose measures add to 180 degrees

look.title: The Open Laptop
look.text: A laptop sits on a desk. The screen is tipped back so that the angle between the screen and the desk behind it is 65 degrees. On the other side, the angle between the keyboard and the screen is the rest of the straight line made by the desk. Now imagine a book propped up so the angle between its cover and the desk is 25 degrees, and someone asks for the angle between the cover and a vertical wall it leans against.
look.prompt: Find both missing angles. Which pair is supplementary, and which is complementary?

check.q: An angle measures 35 degrees. What is its complement?
check.why: Complementary angles add to 90: 90 − 35 = 55 degrees. 145 is the supplement.

check.q: An angle measures 112 degrees. What is its supplement?
check.why: Supplementary angles add to 180: 180 − 112 = 68 degrees. Check: 112 + 68 = 180.

check.q: Two angles measure 40 degrees and 50 degrees. What are they?
choices: Neither, because they do not touch
check.why: 40 + 50 = 90, so they are complementary. Touching does not matter.

lessons.title: When Two Lines Cross
lessons.mainIdea: When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other are equal and the angles next to each other add to 180.
reading: Two straight lines cross like an X and make four angles. The angles across from each other, tip to tip, are called *vertical angles*. Vertical angles are always equal. The angles that share a side and sit next to each other are *adjacent angles*. Adjacent angles on a straight line are supplementary, because together they make a straight line of 180 degrees.

Suppose one angle of the X measures 70 degrees. The angle right next to it, along the same straight line, is 180 − 70 = 110 degrees. The angle across from the 70 is also 70. The angle across from the 110 is also 110. So the four angles are 70, 110, 70, 110, and all four add to 360, a full turn.

Why are vertical angles equal? Call the angles A, B, C and D going around the X. A and B are on a line, so A + B = 180. B and C are on a line too, so B + C = 180. Both A and C equal 180 − B, so A = C. No measuring needed; the straight lines force it.

A common mistake is to assume that adjacent angles are equal because they look similar. They are equal only if each is exactly 90 degrees, which happens when the lines are perpendicular. Otherwise one is smaller and one is larger, and only the pair across the X matches.

words.d: the two angles directly across from each other where two lines cross; they are always equal
two angles that share a side and a corner point, sitting next to each other
two lines that cross at a right angle of 90 degrees

look.title: Scissors
look.text: Open a pair of scissors partway. The two blades and the two handles form an X that meets at the screw. The angle between the two blades is 40 degrees. Someone asks for the angle between the two handles, and then the angle between one blade and the handle on the same side.
look.prompt: What are the two angles? Which pair is vertical and which pair is adjacent?

check.q: Two lines cross. One of the angles is 70 degrees. What is the angle directly across from it?
check.why: Angles across from each other at a crossing are vertical angles, and vertical angles are equal: 70 degrees.

check.q: Two lines cross. One angle is 70 degrees. What is the angle next to it along the same straight line?
check.why: Adjacent angles on a line add to 180: 180 − 70 = 110 degrees.

check.q: Two lines cross and make four angles. What do the four angles add up to?
check.why: Two pairs of supplementary angles: 180 + 180 = 360, one full turn around the crossing point.

lessons.title: Finding Unknown Angles
lessons.mainIdea: Write what the angles must add to as an equation, then solve it to find the unknown.
reading: Many angle problems give a relationship instead of a number. Two angles are supplementary and one is twice the other. What are they? Call the smaller one x. The larger is 2x. Together they make 180, so x + 2x = 180, which is 3x = 180, so x = 60. The angles are 60 and 120. Check: 60 + 120 = 180, and 120 is twice 60.

The same plan works for complementary angles. One angle is four times its complement. Call the small one x, the large one 4x, and write x + 4x = 90. That is 5x = 90, so x = 18. The angles are 18 and 72. Check: 18 + 72 = 90, and 4 × 18 = 72.

Sometimes three or more angles share a line or a point. Three angles sit side by side along a straight line and measure 45, 65 and x. Then 45 + 65 + x = 180, so 110 + x = 180 and x = 70. If angles go all the way around a point, they add to 360 instead.

The main error is stopping too soon. Solving for x gives the small angle. If the question asks for the large angle, multiply. If it asks for both, list both. Always reread the question after you finish the algebra, and always add your answers back together to check the total.

words.d: a math sentence with an equals sign that says two amounts are the same
a number you do not know yet, usually written as a letter like x

look.title: The Pizza Slice
look.text: A pizza is cut into three slices from the center, and the three center angles go all the way around. One slice has a center angle of 150 degrees. The second slice has a center angle exactly twice as big as the third slice. Write an equation for the three angles and solve it.
look.prompt: What are the center angles of the second and third slices? How can you check?

check.q: Two supplementary angles: one is twice the other. What is the larger angle?
check.why: x + 2x = 180, so x = 60 and the larger angle is 2 × 60 = 120 degrees.

check.q: Two complementary angles: one is four times the other. What is the larger angle?
check.why: x + 4x = 90, so 5x = 90 and x = 18. The larger is 4 × 18 = 72 degrees.

check.q: Three angles along a straight line measure 45, 65 and x degrees. What is x?
check.why: 45 + 65 + x = 180, so 110 + x = 180 and x = 70. Adding 45 and 65 gives 110, which is not the answer.

lessons.title: A Line Across Two Parallels
lessons.mainIdea: When a line crosses two parallel lines, it makes matching angles: corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal, and same-side interior angles add to 180.
reading: Two lines are *parallel* if they run in the same direction and never meet, like railroad tracks. A third line that cuts across both is a *transversal*. Where it crosses each track it makes four angles, so eight angles in all. Because the two tracks point the same way, the eight angles come in only two sizes: a small one and a large one that add to 180.

Some pairs have names. *Corresponding angles* sit in the same position at each crossing, like the upper-left angle at the first track and the upper-left angle at the second. They are equal. *Alternate interior angles* lie between the two tracks on opposite sides of the transversal, forming a Z shape. They are equal too. Same-side interior angles lie between the tracks on the same side and add to 180.

Suppose a transversal makes a 130-degree angle at the top track. The corresponding angle at the bottom track is also 130. The angle next to it on the line is 180 − 130 = 50. Every angle in the picture is either 130 or 50. If one alternate interior angle is 55, its partner is 55, and the same-side interior angle across the transversal is 180 − 55 = 125.

This is the fact Eratosthenes used. The sun's rays are parallel lines. The stick in Alexandria and the line from the Earth's center to Syene form a transversal. The shadow angle at the stick equals the angle at the Earth's center, because they are alternate interior angles. The rule works only when the lines really are parallel. If they lean even slightly, the equal pairs stop being equal.

words.d: lines that run in the same direction and never meet, no matter how far they go
a line that crosses two or more other lines
angles in the same position at two different crossings of a transversal; equal when the lines are parallel
angles between two parallel lines on opposite sides of the transversal; they are equal

look.title: Crosswalk Stripes
look.text: The white stripes of a crosswalk are parallel. A bike lane cuts across them at a slant. At the first stripe, the bike lane makes a 40-degree angle on the lower left. Picture the crossing at the second stripe, and then at the tenth stripe far down the street.
look.prompt: What is the lower-left angle at the second stripe? At the tenth? What is the upper-left angle at any stripe?

check.q: A transversal crosses two parallel lines and makes a 130-degree angle at the first line. What is the corresponding angle at the second line?
check.why: Corresponding angles on parallel lines are equal, so 130 degrees. 50 is its supplement.

check.q: One alternate interior angle measures 55 degrees. What does its partner measure?
check.why: Alternate interior angles between parallel lines are equal: 55 degrees.

check.q: Two same-side interior angles lie between parallel lines. One is 55 degrees. What is the other?
check.why: Same-side interior angles add to 180: 180 − 55 = 125 degrees.

lessons.title: Why a Triangle Adds to 180
lessons.mainIdea: The three angles of any triangle add to 180 degrees, because a parallel line through the top corner lines them up along a straight line.
reading: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle and fit them together point to point. They always make a straight line. That is the famous rule: the three angles of any triangle add to 180 degrees. If two angles of a triangle are 48 and 67, the third is 180 − 48 − 67 = 65. Check: 48 + 67 + 65 = 180.

Here is why it is always true. Draw a triangle with corners A at the top, and B and C at the bottom. Through A, draw a line parallel to the bottom side BC. Now the side AB is a transversal crossing two parallel lines, so the angle at B has an equal alternate interior angle up at A, to the left. In the same way, the angle at C has an equal partner at A, to the right. The three angles at A, the left partner, the triangle's own angle, and the right partner, sit along a straight line. Together they make 180. So angle B plus angle A plus angle C is 180.

A right triangle already spends 90 degrees on its square corner, so the other two angles add to 90 and are complementary. If one is 34 degrees, the other is 90 − 34 = 56. In an equilateral triangle, all three angles are equal, so each is 180 ÷ 3 = 60 degrees.

The common error is subtracting only one angle. Given 48 and 67, some students write 180 − 48 = 132 and stop. Subtract both, or add the two known angles first and subtract the sum. Another slip is forgetting that a right angle counts as one of the three.

words.d: a triangle with three equal sides and three 60-degree angles
an angle smaller than 90 degrees

look.title: Two Angles Given, One Missing
look.cite: Third angle = 180 minus the sum of the other two
look.prompt: Check each row by adding all three angles. Which rows describe a right triangle, and which describe a triangle with two equal angles?

check.q: Two angles of a triangle measure 48 and 67 degrees. What is the third angle?
check.why: 48 + 67 = 115, and 180 − 115 = 65 degrees. Subtracting only 48 gives 132.

check.q: A right triangle has one acute angle of 34 degrees. What is the other acute angle?
check.why: The two acute angles add to 180 − 90 = 90, so 90 − 34 = 56 degrees.

check.q: In the proof that a triangle's angles add to 180, why draw a line through the top corner parallel to the base?
choices: To split the triangle into two right triangles
To cut the base in half
So the two base angles have equal partners at the top that line up along a straight line
check.why: Alternate interior angles copy the base angles up to the top corner, where all three angles fill a straight line of 180 degrees.

lessons.title: The Triangle Inequality
lessons.mainIdea: Three lengths make a triangle only if every two of them add to more than the third.
reading: Can you make a triangle from sticks of length 3, 4 and 8? Lay the 8 down. Now try to connect the 3 and the 4 above it so their ends meet. Even lying flat along the 8, they only reach 3 + 4 = 7. They never touch. No triangle. The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest side. That rule is the *triangle inequality*.

The rule says: the sum of any two sides is greater than the third side. It is enough to check the two shortest sides against the longest. Sides 5, 7 and 9: 5 + 7 = 12, which is more than 9, so yes. Sides 2, 3 and 6: 2 + 3 = 5, less than 6, so no. Sides 6, 6 and 12: 6 + 6 = 12, exactly equal, so no. The two short sides lie flat on the long one and the triangle collapses into a line.

The rule also tells you how long a missing side can be. Two sides are 5 and 7. The third side must be less than 5 + 7 = 12, or the other two cannot reach across it. It must also be more than 7 − 5 = 2, or the 5 and the third side together cannot reach across the 7. So the third side is any length strictly between 2 and 12: 3 works, 10 works, 2 and 12 do not.

This is why the shortest path between two points is a straight line. Any detour through a third point turns the trip into two sides of a triangle, and two sides always add to more than the third. Walking the diagonal across a park is shorter than walking around two edges for exactly this reason.

words.d: the rule that any two sides of a triangle must add to more than the third side
a statement that one amount is greater than or less than another, using > or <

look.title: Three Straws
look.text: You have straws cut to 4 inches, 6 inches and 11 inches. You try to make a triangle and cannot. You are allowed to trim the longest straw. You want to know how much you must cut off before the three straws will finally form a triangle, and what the very first working length would look like.
look.prompt: How long can the longest straw be at most? What happens at exactly that length?

check.q: Can sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm form a triangle?
choices: No, because 8 is an even number
check.why: The two shorter sides must add to more than the longest: 3 + 4 = 7, which is less than 8.

check.q: Two sides of a triangle are 5 m and 7 m. Which of these could be the third side?
check.why: The third side must be between 7 − 5 = 2 and 5 + 7 = 12, not including 2 and 12. Only 10 fits.

check.q: Sides of 6, 6 and 12 do not make a triangle. Why?
choices: 6 + 6 = 12 exactly, so the two short sides lie flat along the long one
check.why: The sum must be greater than the third side, not equal. Equal means the shape collapses into a straight line.

lessons.title: One Triangle, Many or None
lessons.mainIdea: Some sets of measurements build exactly one triangle, some build many different sizes, and some build none at all.
reading: Give a builder three side lengths, say 5, 6 and 7 cm. Draw the 7 as the base. Set a compass to 5 and draw an arc from the left end, then set it to 6 and draw an arc from the right end. The arcs cross at exactly one point above the base. Connect it, and you have the triangle. Anyone who follows these steps gets the same triangle, just possibly flipped or turned. Three sides fix a triangle completely.

Now give a builder three angles instead, 30, 60 and 90 degrees. You can draw a tiny triangle with those angles or a huge one. All of them have the same shape, but they are different sizes. Three angles alone build many triangles, not one. You would need at least one side length to pin down the size.

Some instructions build nothing. Angles of 100, 50 and 40 degrees add to 190, more than 180, so no triangle has them. Sides 3, 4 and 8 fail the triangle inequality. And some sets fall in between. Two sides and the angle between them fix one triangle. Two sides and an angle not between them can sometimes fit two different triangles.

Before you start drawing, sort the request. Do the angles add to 180? Do the sides pass the triangle inequality? Is there at least one side length? Those three questions tell you whether to expect one triangle, many or none.

words.d: a drawing tool with a point and a pencil that draws arcs and circles of a set size
a curved piece of a circle

look.title: Orders at the Metal Shop
look.text: A metal shop gets three orders for triangular brackets. Order A asks for sides 8, 15 and 17 cm. Order B asks for angles 45, 45 and 90 with no lengths. Order C asks for sides 4, 5 and 10 cm. The shop manager must decide which orders can be made exactly as written, which need more information, and which must be sent back.
look.prompt: Sort the three orders and explain each decision with a rule from this lesson.

check.q: A triangle must have sides of 5 cm, 6 cm and 7 cm. How many different triangles fit this description?
check.why: Three side lengths that pass the triangle inequality build exactly one triangle. 5 + 6 = 11 is more than 7, so it exists.

check.q: A triangle must have angles of 30, 60 and 90 degrees. How many different triangles fit?
choices: Many, all the same shape but different sizes
check.why: Angles fix the shape but not the size. Any size works, so there are many.

check.q: A triangle must have angles of 100, 50 and 40 degrees. How many fit?
choices: None, because the angles add to 190
check.why: 100 + 50 + 40 = 190, but a triangle's angles must add to exactly 180. No triangle exists.

lessons.title: Slicing Solids
lessons.mainIdea: A cross section is the flat shape you see when you slice a solid, and it depends on the direction of the cut.
reading: Cut a block of cheese and look at the cut face. That flat shape is a *cross section*. Slice a rectangular block straight across, parallel to one end, and the cross section is a rectangle the same size as that end. Slice a cylinder of cheese parallel to its round base and you get a circle. Slice the same cylinder straight down through its center, along its length, and you get a rectangle.

Pyramids and cones change with height. A square pyramid sliced parallel to its base gives a square, and the square gets smaller as the slice moves up toward the point. Sliced straight down through the top point and the middle of the base, the same pyramid gives a triangle. A cone sliced parallel to its base gives a circle; sliced through its tip and straight down, a triangle.

A cube sliced parallel to a face gives a square. But tilt the blade. Slicing a cube corner to corner through opposite edges gives a rectangle that is longer than it is wide. Slicing off one corner gives a triangle. Some slices of a cube even give a hexagon, a six-sided shape, when the blade passes through the middle of six edges.

Cross sections show up everywhere. A doctor's scan is a stack of cross sections of a body. An architect's floor plan is a horizontal cross section of a building. A slice of an orange is a circle because an orange is a sphere, and every straight slice of a sphere is a circle.

words.d: the flat shape you see on the cut face when a solid is sliced straight through
a flat shape with six straight sides

look.title: The Deli Counter
look.text: A deli worker has three loaves on the counter: a long rectangular loaf, a round cylinder of bologna, and a cone-shaped wedge of cheese standing on its wide end. A customer asks for slices, and the worker can cut each one either straight across, parallel to its end or base, or lengthwise straight down through the center.
look.prompt: Describe the six possible slice shapes: two for each loaf. Which two loaves can both give a rectangle?

check.q: A cylinder is sliced parallel to its circular base. What is the cross section?
check.why: A slice parallel to the base matches the base, which is a circle.

check.q: A square pyramid is sliced parallel to its base, halfway up. What is the cross section?
choices: A square smaller than the base
A square the same size as the base
check.why: Slices parallel to the base are squares that shrink toward the point, so it is a smaller square.

check.q: A cylinder is sliced straight down through the center along its length. What is the cross section?
check.why: Cutting along the length shows the full height and the full width, which makes a rectangle.

lessons.title: Reading a Scale
lessons.mainIdea: A scale tells how a length on a drawing matches a real length, and multiplying or dividing by that ratio converts between them.
reading: A *scale drawing* shows something real, like a room or a city, shrunk or enlarged so every length changes by the same amount. The *scale* tells you the match. A floor plan with a scale of 1 cm : 4 m means every centimeter on paper stands for 4 meters in the building. The shape stays the same; only the size changes.

To go from drawing to real, multiply. A wall that is 6 cm long on the plan is 6 × 4 = 24 m in real life. A wall that is 7.5 cm on the plan is 7.5 × 4 = 30 m. To go from real to drawing, divide. A real hallway of 50 m appears as 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 cm on the plan. Check by going back: 12.5 × 4 = 50.

Maps use scales too. A road map with a scale of 1 inch : 20 miles shows two towns 180 miles apart as 180 ÷ 20 = 9 inches apart on the paper. A model car built at 1 : 24 is one twenty-fourth of the real size, so a real car 4.8 m long becomes a model 4.8 ÷ 24 = 0.2 m, or 20 cm.

The common error is going the wrong direction, dividing when you should multiply. Ask which is bigger. If the drawing is smaller than the real thing, real lengths must come out larger than drawing lengths. If your real wall comes out shorter than the drawing, you divided by mistake.

words.d: a drawing of a real object with every length shrunk or enlarged by the same ratio
the ratio between a length on a drawing and the real length it stands for, like 1 cm : 4 m

look.title: A Floor Plan at 1 cm : 4 m
rows: classroom wall, 2.5 cm on the plan
look.cite: Real length = plan length × 4 at a scale of 1 cm : 4 m
look.prompt: Check each row by multiplying. A new room is 18 m long in real life. How long would it be on this plan?

check.q: A floor plan uses a scale of 1 cm : 4 m. A wall is 7.5 cm long on the plan. How long is the real wall?
check.why: Drawing to real means multiply: 7.5 × 4 = 30 m.

check.q: On that same plan, how long would a real 50 m hallway be drawn?
check.why: Real to drawing means divide: 50 ÷ 4 = 12.5 cm. Check: 12.5 × 4 = 50.

check.q: A map has a scale of 1 inch : 20 miles. Two towns are 180 miles apart. How far apart are they on the map?
check.why: 180 ÷ 20 = 9 inches on the map. Multiplying instead gives 3600.

lessons.title: Scale Factor and Area
lessons.mainIdea: When every length is multiplied by a scale factor, the area is multiplied by the scale factor squared.
reading: A *scale factor* is the single number every length gets multiplied by. Enlarging a photo by a scale factor of 3 makes every length three times as long. A rectangle 2 cm by 5 cm becomes 6 cm by 15 cm. But look at the areas. The original covers 2 × 5 = 10 cm². The copy covers 6 × 15 = 90 cm². The area is not 3 times bigger. It is 9 times bigger.

That always happens, because area has two dimensions and both get multiplied. Scale factor 3 makes the area 3 × 3 = 9 times bigger. Scale factor 2 makes it 2 × 2 = 4 times bigger. A garden of 12 m² enlarged by a scale factor of 2 becomes 12 × 4 = 48 m². Going the other way, a scale factor of 1/2 makes each length half as long and the area 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 as large.

This explains the pizza puzzle from the last chapter. A 12-inch pizza has twice the diameter of a 6-inch pizza, a scale factor of 2, so it has four times the area. It also matters for cost. If a poster twice as wide and twice as tall costs the same per square foot, it costs four times as much, not twice as much.

The mistake is to multiply the area by the scale factor itself. If a drawing at 1 cm : 4 m shows a room as 5 cm by 6 cm, the plan area is 30 cm². The real room is 20 m by 24 m, so 480 m². That is 30 × 16, because 4 × 4 = 16, not 30 × 4 = 120.

words.d: the number every length is multiplied by to make a scaled copy
to make a copy bigger with a scale factor greater than 1
to make a copy smaller with a scale factor less than 1, like 1/2

look.title: One Square, Many Sizes
look.cite: Area of a square with side equal to the scale factor times 1 cm
look.prompt: What is the pattern between the scale factor and the area? What area would a scale factor of 7 give?

check.q: A 2 cm by 5 cm rectangle is enlarged by a scale factor of 3. How many times larger is the new area?
check.why: The new rectangle is 6 by 15, area 90, versus 10 before. 90 ÷ 10 = 9, which is 3 squared.

check.q: A garden has an area of 12 m². It is enlarged by a scale factor of 2. What is the new area?
check.why: Area grows by the scale factor squared: 2 × 2 = 4, and 12 × 4 = 48 m².

check.q: A blueprint is reduced with a scale factor of 1/2. What happens to the area?
check.why: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. Both the length and the width are halved.

review.q: An angle measures 27 degrees. What are its complement and its supplement?
Two lines cross. One angle is 115 degrees. What are the other three?
review.why: The vertical angle is 115. The two adjacent angles are each 180 − 115 = 65.

review.q: Two supplementary angles: one is 5 times the other. What is the smaller angle?
review.why: x + 5x = 180, so 6x = 180 and x = 30 degrees. The larger is 150.

review.q: A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One angle is 72 degrees. Which statement is true?
choices: Its alternate interior angle is 18 degrees
Every angle in the figure is 72 degrees
Its corresponding angle is 72 degrees and its same-side interior angle is 108 degrees
review.why: Corresponding angles are equal, and same-side interior angles add to 180: 180 − 72 = 108.

review.q: Two angles of a triangle are 35 and 85 degrees. What is the third?
Which set of side lengths can form a triangle?
review.why: 4 + 5 = 9 is greater than 8. The other sets have two sides that add to the third or less.

review.q: A model of a bridge uses a scale of 1 cm : 25 m. The model is 14 cm long. How long is the real bridge?
review.why: 14 × 25 = 350 m. Model to real means multiply.

review.q: A photo is enlarged with a scale factor of 4. Its area becomes how many times larger?
review.why: Area is multiplied by the scale factor squared: 4 × 4 = 16.
